case_facts: A refrigerator I bought caught fire within a week from a manufacturing defect, damaging my kitchen; the company refuses to compensate me.

analysis.summary: A consumer purchased a refrigerator that caught fire within one week of purchase due to an alleged manufacturing defect, causing damage to the buyer's kitchen. The manufacturer has refused to provide any compensation for the product failure or consequential property damage. The case involves product liability, deficiency in service, and unfair trade practice under consumer protection law.

issues.issue: Whether the fire caused by the refrigerator constitutes a 'defect in goods' entitling the consumer to replacement or refund
Whether the manufacturer's refusal to compensate amounts to 'deficiency in service' and 'unfair trade practice'
Whether the manufacturer is strictly liable under product liability provisions for damage caused by a defective product
Whether the consumer is entitled to compensation for consequential property damage (kitchen damage) arising from the defective product
issues.governing_law: Consumer Protection Act 2019, Section 89; Sale of Goods Act 1930, Section 16

governing_acts: Sale of Goods Act 1930 Section 16 implied warranty

transcript.speaker: ai
transcript.argument:
Your Lordship, I appear on behalf of the Complainant, a consumer who purchased a refrigerator in good faith, only to have it burst into flames within a mere seven days of purchase — not through any misuse, not through any negligence on his part, but solely on account of a manufacturing defect embedded in the product by the Respondent company. The kitchen of my client was damaged, his family was endangered, and the Respondent has had the audacity to refuse any compensation whatsoever. This Court is called upon today to send an unequivocal message: a manufacturer cannot place a defective, hazardous product into the stream of commerce and then wash its hands of the consequences.

Your Lordship, the Respondent is a commercial enterprise engaged in the manufacture and sale of electrical appliances — devices that draw power and, when defectively made, become instruments of destruction inside a consumer's home. This is precisely the scenario addressed by this Hon'ble Supreme Court in **M.C. Mehta v. Union of India** (docid: 6033120), where the Court evolved the doctrine of **absolute liability** — holding that an enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity bears an absolute and non-delegable duty to compensate for harm caused, with no exceptions available. A refrigerator with a defective electrical component that spontaneously combusts is, by any measure, an inherently dangerous instrumentality. The Respondent cannot hide behind pleas of due diligence or quality checks; absolute liability admits of no such escape.

Your Lordship, this principle is powerfully reinforced by the **polluter-pays principle** as articulated in **Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India** (docid: 7012009), where the Court held that the financial cost of preventing or remedying damage caused by an activity must be borne by the party responsible for the harm. The Respondent manufactured the defective unit; the Respondent introduced it into commerce; the Respondent is the author of my client's loss. It is the Respondent, and the Respondent alone, who must bear the full cost of remedying that damage — including repair of the kitchen, replacement of the appliance, and appropriate compensation for the mental agony and harassment suffered.

Your Lordship, the facts here are stark and uncontroverted: a brand-new refrigerator, a manufacturing defect, a fire within seven days, and a company that refuses to acknowledge its responsibility. The law is equally clear. I respectfully submit that this Court should hold the Respondent liable under the doctrine of absolute liability, direct full compensatory relief to my client, and impose such additional costs as this Forum deems fit to deter such callous disregard for consumer safety. I shall demonstrate, as these proceedings unfold, that there is no defence available to the Respondent in law or in equity.
